input.question: How is it that your veins/arteries don't simply cut off whenever you sit or compress the body in normal circumstances?
input.ground_truth: For the most part veins and arteries are not on the surface so simply sitting won't compress them enough to "cut off" flow, but it can be significant enough to reduce flow to the point your leg "goes to sleep" , also why you should not have legs crossed when taking your blood pressure, etc. Also the circulatory system is remarkably complex and closing one pathway often is compensated for by blood rerouting through alternate, less restricted, paths.

Question: How is it that your veins/arteries don't simply cut off whenever you sit or compress the body in normal circumstances?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine your blood vessels—like the tubes that carry water in your house—are very smart and strong.

When you sit or squeeze your leg, it might look like you are squishing those tubes, but they are really tough and flexible. They can bend and move a little bit without getting closed up.

Also, your body is really good at making sure blood keeps moving. There are little doors called "valves" inside your veins that help the blood flow in the right direction, like a swing door that only opens one way. So even if you sit or press on your leg, the blood can still get through those doors and keep moving.

That’s why your blood doesn’t just stop flowing when you sit or squeeze yourself! Your body is super smart and takes care of it.
